paragraphs: The paper asks how much information an algorithm must obtain to choose a good group of k elements from n candidates. Its main setting involves monotone submodular objectives, where adding elements cannot reduce value and additional elements offer diminishing returns. The question is whether a constant-factor approximation can use substantially fewer than n queries to the objective.

The authors prove a lower bound that is nearly linear in n, strengthening an earlier bound proportional to n/k. Here, “nearly” allows polylogarithmic factors. The result applies even when the algorithm only estimates the best achievable value, without identifying a subset that achieves it. This makes the information requirement relevant to both optimization and value estimation.

For additive objectives, the paper identifies a different relationship between these tasks. Finding an approximately optimal subset still needs nearly linear query complexity, but estimating its value takes roughly n/k queries, up to polylogarithmic factors. The matching bounds establish when estimating an answer can be substantially cheaper than constructing one.
icml-2025-a-near-linear-query-lower-boun.tldr: Nearly linear query complexity is required for constant-factor submodular maximization, even for value estimation, while additive objectives permit cheaper value estimates.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models make predictions through human-understandable concepts, making those concepts central to how the system reaches a decision. Their training commonly assumes that the supplied concept labels are accurate. This paper examines what happens when that assumption fails and shows that mislabeled concepts can substantially reduce model performance.

The proposed response is Concept Preference Optimization, or CPO, a training objective derived from Direct Preference Optimization. It changes how the model learns concepts from imperfect supervision. The authors analyze the objective and show that it directly optimizes the concept’s posterior distribution. They also compare its sensitivity to concept noise with that of Binary Cross Entropy, the alternative loss considered in the paper.

The analysis finds CPO inherently less sensitive to concept noise, and experiments support that comparison. Across three real-world datasets, CPO consistently outperforms Binary Cross Entropy both with and without additional label noise. The contribution addresses the reliability of the concept-learning stage, which matters because interpretable intermediate concepts are useful only insofar as the model learns them effectively.
icml-2025-addressing-concept-mislabeling.tldr: Concept Preference Optimization improves concept bottleneck learning by reducing sensitivity to mislabeled concepts.

paragraphs: Neural networks often represent high-dimensional inputs using features organized around lower-dimensional structures, or manifolds. This paper connects those learned structures to computational algebra. It uses vanishing ideals, collections of polynomials that vanish on a structure, to characterize the class-specific manifolds found inside a trained network.

The proposed architecture keeps a pretrained network only up to an intermediate layer. It then approximates each class manifold using polynomial generators of its vanishing ideal. A single polynomial layer converts the intermediate representations into features that can be separated linearly. This replaces a deeper portion of the network with a transformation designed around the geometry already present in its hidden representations.

The resulting models have substantially fewer layers and parameters while retaining comparable accuracy and achieving higher throughput. The authors also use spectral complexity analysis to derive generalization guarantees that can, in principle, be tighter than those for standard deep networks. Numerical experiments support the approach’s effectiveness and efficiency, connecting the algebraic construction to practical model simplification.
icml-2025-approximating-latent-manifolds.tldr: Polynomial descriptions of learned class manifolds let the authors replace network layers while preserving comparable accuracy and improving efficiency.

paragraphs: ECG signals describe physiological activity, while accompanying reports provide textual interpretations. Learning from both could strengthen automated ECG interpretation, but the two kinds of data differ substantially and labeled examples can be scarce. D-BETA addresses this problem by pretraining representations that connect ECG signals with text.

The framework combines a masked auto-encoder with contrastive learning. Masked modality modeling supplies a generative learning task, while the discriminative components help distinguish and align information across the two modalities. Specialized losses and an improved negative sampling strategy support this alignment. The combination aims to make the learned representations useful for downstream decisions as well as for the pretraining tasks.

Experiments cover five public datasets and several downstream tasks. The authors report an average AUC improvement of 15% in linear probing using only one percent of training data, and a 2% improvement in zero-shot performance over state-of-the-art models. These findings support the usefulness of joint ECG-text representations when downstream supervision is scarce or absent, while the clinical application remains a stated potential.
icml-2025-boosting-masked-ecg-text-auto-.tldr: D-BETA combines masked reconstruction and contrastive learning to improve ECG-text representations for low-data and zero-shot tasks.

paragraphs: Protective perturbations add imperceptible changes to images to interfere with unauthorized customization of latent diffusion models. Their intended role is to prevent a model from learning effectively from those images. This paper studies both why these protections work and whether they remain effective when the customization procedure adapts to them.

Qualitative and quantitative experiments identify distortion of latent representations as the primary reason the protective examples succeed. This connects the visible training images to the internal representations used by latent diffusion models. Building on that finding, the authors introduce Contrastive Adversarial Training, or CAT, which uses lightweight adapters as an adaptive attack against the protections.

Across extensive experiments, CAT substantially reduces the effectiveness of protective perturbations during customization. The result exposes a weakness in the evaluated protections when they face an adaptive training method. The paper therefore contributes both a mechanism-level explanation and a robustness test: it argues that protective perturbations need stronger evaluation and improvement before their effectiveness against ordinary customization can be treated as evidence of resilience to adaptation.
icml-2025-cat-contrastive-adversarial-tr.tldr: CAT uses lightweight adapters to weaken protective image perturbations, exposing their vulnerability to adaptive diffusion-model customization.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks implant unwanted behavior into a neural network during training. Existing purification methods often depend on labeled data or particular training procedures, which complicates their use outside supervised learning. This paper proposes Two-stage Symmetry Connectivity, or TSC, to make purification applicable across different learning settings while requiring only a small fraction of clean samples.

TSC uses permutation invariance in neural networks together with quadratic mode connectivity. These properties concern symmetries and connections in the network’s weight space. The authors prove that their construction increases loss on poisoned samples while maintaining a bound on clean accuracy. The theoretical argument links changes in the model’s weights to a selective disruption of backdoor behavior.

Experiments show defense performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches in supervised learning. The method also extends to self-supervised frameworks, including SimCLR and CLIP, where it retains strong defense capabilities. Its significance lies in that broader applicability: purification is organized around properties of neural network weights and does not depend on a particular data format.
icml-2025-circumventing-backdoor-space-v.tldr: TSC exploits neural network weight symmetries to purify backdoors across supervised and self-supervised settings using a small amount of clean data.

paragraphs: Many generative modeling and stochastic control tasks require steering a diffusion process toward desirable outcomes at its final time. Existing methods commonly use gradients of a differentiable reward. That becomes problematic for singular rewards, such as a diffusion-bridge target whose reward is infinite when the target is reached and zero otherwise.

The paper develops a framework based on Malliavin calculus to handle such singularities. Its central construction generalizes the Tweedie score formula to nonlinear stochastic differential equations. This provides a mathematical basis for conditioning methods that remain usable when ordinary reward gradients cannot supply the needed guidance. Applications include diffusion bridges and adding conditional controls to an already trained diffusion model.

The authors report stable, reliable training and performance exceeding existing techniques. They also derive a new score-matching objective as a byproduct of the framework. Their loss formulations could readily be extended to diffusions on manifolds or in infinite-dimensional spaces; the abstract presents these as possible extensions, alongside the demonstrated benefits for conditioning diffusion processes.
icml-2025-conditioning-diffusions-using-.tldr: A Malliavin-calculus framework enables diffusion conditioning with singular terminal rewards and supports stable training.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees when data are exchangeable. Corruption in individual entries of a test example can undermine that condition. This paper addresses such cellwise outliers, where the difficulty comes from contaminated features rather than necessarily from an entirely unusable example.

The proposed framework first detects suspicious feature entries and then replaces them through imputation. Crucially, it also adaptively applies detection and imputation to the calibration data. That additional step accounts for uncertainty in the processed test features and constructs exchangeable features for forming the test-label interval. The method therefore connects data repair with the calibration procedure needed for uncertainty guarantees.

The authors develop two algorithms, PDI-CP and JDI-CP, and analyze distribution-free coverage under commonly used detection and imputation procedures. In particular, JDI-CP has a finite-sample coverage guarantee of 1−2α. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show robust coverage and efficiency comparable to an oracle baseline, supporting the value of coordinating outlier handling with conformal calibration.
icml-2025-conformal-prediction-with-cell.tldr: Coordinating outlier detection and imputation with conformal calibration supports reliable prediction intervals for partially corrupted test features.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based purification tries to remove adversarial image perturbations by adding noise and then reconstructing a clean image. This can also damage meaningful image information. The paper examines that tradeoff in the frequency domain, separating images into amplitude and phase spectra to study where adversarial damage is concentrated.

The authors find that damage in both spectra tends to increase with frequency. Lower-frequency components can therefore retain useful content and structural information. Their theoretical analysis indicates that existing purification methods damage frequencies indiscriminately. The proposed method instead reuses relatively preserved information from the adversarial input during each step of reverse diffusion.

For amplitude, the method replaces the estimated image’s low-frequency components with corresponding components from the input. For phase, it constrains the estimated values to a designated range around the input’s phase, emphasizing low frequencies. Extensive experiments show significant improvements over most current defenses. The findings support frequency-aware reconstruction as a way to remove perturbations while better preserving the information needed to recognize the original image.
icml-2025-diffusion-based-adversarial-pu.tldr: Preserving relatively intact low-frequency amplitude and phase information improves diffusion-based adversarial image purification.

paragraphs: The Discrete Markov Probabilistic Model, or DMPM, generates data directly in a discrete state space. Its forward noising process is a continuous-time Markov chain: a Poissonian clock triggers random label flips. This process can be sampled exactly, giving the model an explicit way to corrupt discrete data before learning how to reverse that corruption.

The reverse process also proceeds through jumps. Its jump intensity is controlled by a discrete counterpart of the score function used in score-based generation. The authors prove that this intensity can be expressed as a conditional expectation of a function of the forward process. That relationship strengthens the mathematical connection between discrete generation and the score-based framework.

The paper establishes convergence bounds under minimal assumptions and evaluates generation on low-dimensional Bernoulli datasets and high-dimensional binary MNIST data. The reported results show strong performance on these discrete structures. Together, the construction and analysis provide a theoretically grounded route from an exactly sampled noising process to a practical discrete generative algorithm.
icml-2025-discrete-markov-probabilistic-.tldr: DMPM builds discrete generation around reversible jump processes, with a score-based interpretation and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Evaluating defenses against prompt attacks requires accounting for attackers who adapt over multiple interactions and legitimate users who still need useful responses. The paper argues that existing evaluations often overlook both considerations. It introduces D-SEC, a threat model that separates the two groups, represents multi-step interactions, and expresses security and utility in a form that can be optimized.

The authors also introduce Gandalf, a gamified platform that crowdsources adaptive attacks. They collect and release 279,000 prompt attacks and analyze them alongside benign user data. This combination supports evaluation of how defenses affect adversarial behavior and ordinary use within the same broader security-utility problem.

The analysis finds that defenses built into an LLM, including system prompts, can reduce usability even when they do not explicitly block requests. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of restricted application domains, defense in depth, and adaptive defenses. The practical implication is that a useful security evaluation must examine the quality of legitimate interactions as well as resistance to attacks.
icml-2025-gandalf-the-red-adaptive-secur.tldr: D-SEC and Gandalf evaluate adaptive prompt attacks together with the usability costs that defenses impose on legitimate users.

paragraphs: Predicting nearby agents’ motion in autonomous driving requires representing several plausible futures. GoIRL approaches this through inverse reinforcement learning, using contextual information to infer rewards and a policy from which multiple plans can be sampled. Its design connects vectorized road context with a framework for modeling uncertain behavior.

A feature adaptor aggregates lane-graph features into a grid representation suitable for maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning. The inferred reward distribution supports a policy that generates plausible plans. A hierarchical parameterized generator then produces trajectories conditioned on those sampled plans, with a refinement module intended to improve prediction accuracy.

The framework also uses probability fusion to increase prediction confidence. Experiments on the Argoverse and nuScenes motion forecasting benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance and better generalization than existing supervised models. These results support the approach of combining context-aware reward inference, plan sampling, and trajectory refinement to handle the multiple possible behaviors that make motion forecasting difficult.
icml-2025-goirl-graph-oriented-inverse-r.tldr: GoIRL combines lane-graph context, inverse reinforcement learning, and trajectory refinement to predict multiple plausible agent movements.

paragraphs: LLMs can help plan robotic actions, but complex tasks become difficult when they require many steps and specialized external knowledge. This paper integrates hierarchical planning, knowledge-graph retrieval, and symbolic verification into a single planning approach. The goal is to make the resulting plans more reliable through coordination among these components.

Knowledge Graph-based RAG supplies information for generating a hierarchy of plans. Complex tasks are divided into subtasks, which are expanded into executable atomic actions. A Symbolic Validator checks formal correctness and the decomposition of tasks. It also detects failures by comparing the world state expected from a plan with the state actually observed.

Evaluation across tasks of different complexity and several LLMs shows consistent, significant advantages over baseline methods. The paper also introduces an experimental setup and metrics for examining reasoning and compositional capabilities. Its contribution is the integrated relationship between knowledge retrieval, task decomposition, and validation: retrieved knowledge informs planning, while symbolic checks assess whether the resulting structure and execution fit the expected world state.
icml-2025-hierarchical-planning-for-comp.tldr: Combining knowledge-graph retrieval, hierarchical planning, and symbolic validation improves LLM planning across tasks and models.

paragraphs: This paper develops a generative framework for functions represented by neural networks. It combines Implicit Neural Representations, or INRs, with a Transformer-based hypernetwork: a decoder that produces the parameters of another network from a latent variable. The design addresses representation capacity and computational efficiency challenges associated with earlier MLP-based hypernetworks.

To extend latent diffusion models to INR generation, the authors replace the usual decoder with this Transformer hypernetwork. The resulting system can be trained from scratch. Alternatively, a procedure called hyper-transforming adapts only the decoder while keeping a pretrained latent space frozen, allowing an existing generative model to produce INR representations without full retraining.

Validation across multiple modalities shows improvements in scalability, expressiveness, and generalization over existing INR-based generative models. The significance is both representational and practical: the framework generates structured functions through their network parameters, and the decoder-only adaptation route provides a way to reuse pretrained latent representations. The reported findings support a flexible framework that applies across the tested modalities.
icml-2025-hyper-transforming-latent-diff.tldr: Transformer hypernetworks adapt latent diffusion models to generate implicit neural representations, including through decoder-only fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain structured information that can change across space and time, making watermarking more complicated than for static text or images. KGMark is a framework for placing diffusion fingerprints in dynamic knowledge graphs. It aims to make these fingerprints detectable and robust while preserving transparency in the marked data.

The framework addresses graph variation through several coordinated mechanisms. A clustering-based alignment method adapts the watermark to spatial changes. Redundant embedding strengthens the watermark against attacks and helps it withstand temporal variation. A learnable mask matrix improves fingerprint transparency, addressing another requirement alongside detectability and robustness.

Experiments on multiple public benchmarks support KGMark’s effectiveness. The contribution is a watermarking design that explicitly accounts for the changing structure of graph data, with different components addressing alignment, persistence, and transparency. This matters for the paper’s motivating uses of watermarking, including intellectual property protection and reducing potential harm associated with AI-generated content, where a fingerprint needs to remain useful as the underlying structured data varies.
icml-2025-kgmark-a-diffusion-watermark-f.tldr: KGMark combines alignment, redundant embedding, and learnable masking to watermark knowledge graphs that change over space and time.

paragraphs: Mechanistic PDE Networks learn representations of spatial and temporal data using partial differential equations inside a neural network. In the hidden representation, the equations are linear and can depend on space and time. The model solves these equations and decodes their solutions for a particular task, making equation-based dynamics part of its internal computation.

Efficiently solving those hidden equations is a central challenge. The authors develop a sparse, parallel multigrid solver for linear PDEs that supports GPUs and differentiation. It functions as a module within the network, allowing the equation-solving step to participate in learning while addressing computation and memory costs.

Using this solver, the paper proposes an architecture for discovering nonlinear governing equations in complex settings with robustness to noise. The linear equations in hidden space therefore support a discovery task involving nonlinear dynamics. Validation includes reaction-diffusion and Navier-Stokes equations. The work links a trainable representation of dynamics with a specialized numerical solver, enabling equation discovery through a model that explicitly solves PDEs during its computation.
icml-2025-mechanistic-pde-networks-for-d.tldr: Mechanistic PDE Networks use hidden-space linear PDEs and a differentiable multigrid solver to discover nonlinear governing equations from data.

paragraphs: Combining medical data sources is difficult when their usefulness varies across patients and diseases. Differences in collection time, location, or reagents can also create quality differences between modalities, described here as a Modality Batch Effect. The paper proposes Adaptive Modality Token Re-Balancing, or AMC, to make fusion responsive to those differences.

AMC first assesses the importance and quality of each input modality, then uses that assessment to control the tokens entering fusion. More important modalities retain more informative tokens. Uninformative tokens are replaced with inter-modal tokens, and self-attention integrates the resulting mixture. This gives the initial quality assessment a direct role in determining what information the fusion stage receives.

Experiments on medical and general multimodal datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness and generalizability. The central contribution is an adaptive connection between modality quality and token allocation. Rather than assuming that a modality contributes equally across all inputs, the framework changes the representation supplied to fusion according to its assessed importance for the particular input.
icml-2025-modalities-contribute-unequall.tldr: AMC adapts multimodal fusion by retaining more informative tokens from higher-quality modalities and replacing uninformative ones.

paragraphs: Noise Conditional Variational Score Distillation, or NCVSD, transfers knowledge from pretrained diffusion models into generative denoisers. These denoisers approximate samples from a denoising posterior across many noise levels. The method builds on the finding that an unconditional score function implicitly characterizes the scores of those posterior distributions.

The authors incorporate that relationship into Variational Score Distillation. At high noise levels, the learned denoiser supports one-step generation starting from Gaussian noise. It also permits multiple sampling steps to improve quality when more inference computation is available. A further property is zero-shot probabilistic inference, supporting flexible and controllable sampling.

Experiments examine class-conditional image generation and inverse problems. With increased test-time computation, NCVSD outperforms its teacher diffusion models and matches larger consistency models. For inverse problems, the authors report record-breaking LPIPS results with substantially fewer function evaluations than diffusion-based methods. These findings support a distillation approach that offers fast generation while retaining the ability to refine samples through additional computation.
icml-2025-noise-conditional-variational-.tldr: NCVSD distills diffusion models into denoisers supporting one-step generation, iterative improvement, and zero-shot probabilistic inference.

paragraphs: Pseudo-labeling expands training data using a model’s own predictions. Common approaches favor predictions that are confident and stable during training. This paper studies a different pattern: examples initially assigned to one category that switch to another in later epochs. The authors call these two-phase labels and investigate their value as additional supervision.

Case studies indicate that these changing predictions contain information about decision boundaries. To identify them, the authors develop a 2-phasic metric that characterizes their spatial and temporal patterns. They also introduce a loss tailored to learning from these labels, allowing the model to reinforce correct correlations and eliminate false ones.

Experiments on eight datasets show that incorporating two-phase labels boosts existing pseudo-labeling methods. The reported average classification accuracy gains are 1.73% on image datasets and 1.92% on graph datasets. The result supports treating a structured change in predictions as potentially useful evidence. It does not require assuming that every unstable prediction is informative; the contribution centers on identifying and learning from this particular two-phase pattern.
icml-2025-non-stationary-predictions-may.tldr: Predictions that switch categories in a two-phase training pattern can supply useful pseudo-labels and improve existing methods.

paragraphs: A single visualization of high-dimensional data can obscure structure when several latent processes influence different observed features. This paper considers settings where the features can be divided into nonoverlapping groups, each expressing a different smooth substructure. It proposes discovering those groups and learning separate embeddings to make the underlying processes easier to interpret.

The partitioning method solves an optimization problem that encourages smoothness measured through graph Laplacians. This favors feature groups with simpler geometric structure. By incorporating partitioning into embedding, the framework generalizes traditional visualization methods so that they can learn multiple representations simultaneously, each associated with its own subset of features.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for identifying the correct subsets when independent or partially dependent manifolds occupy distinct feature subsets. That structural condition is central to the stated guarantee. Experiments on simulated and real data demonstrate extraction of multiple low-dimensional structures and partially independent processes. The contribution is a way to reveal several organized views of the same observations when a combined embedding may distort them.
icml-2025-partition-first-embed-later-la.tldr: Partitioning features by graph-based smoothness enables multiple embeddings that reveal distinct latent structures in high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness, or IBDR, is a Bayesian inference framework aimed at improving ensembles when fine-tuning foundation models. It explicitly models interactions between particles, the members used in its ensemble representation. Those interactions promote greater particle diversity, which the paper connects to improved ensemble quality.

The framework’s theoretical basis relates distributional population loss to an approximate posterior. From this relationship, the authors motivate a practical dual optimization procedure that pursues distributional robustness while encouraging diversity. Robustness and interactions among particles are therefore built into the same inference approach. The method makes the relationships between ensemble members part of the optimization problem.

The authors evaluate IBDR against baseline methods on VTAB-1K and a common reasoning language task. They report consistent improvements over the compared methods. These findings support the practical value of encouraging particle diversity through the proposed Bayesian robustness framework across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a theoretical connection between loss and posterior approximation with an optimization procedure and empirical evidence for improved ensemble performance.
icml-2025-promoting-ensemble-diversity-w.tldr: IBDR models interactions among Bayesian ensemble particles to promote diversity and improve foundation-model fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A prediction about a social event can influence the event itself. People may change their expectations and actions after hearing it, altering the likelihood of the predicted outcome. This paper revisits whether accurate prediction remains possible when forecasts participate in shaping the data they are supposed to predict.

The authors combine ideas from performative prediction and outcome indistinguishability to give a modern theoretical answer. Within their framework, they establish that accurate social predictions can always be produced efficiently, regardless of how predictions affect the data. The result addresses the feedback between forecasts and outcomes directly, showing that such influence does not by itself rule out the accuracy considered in their analysis.

The paper also shows that achievable predictions are often undesirable. This exposes a gap between satisfying previous prediction criteria and obtaining predictions one would want a social system to use. Its contribution therefore includes both an existence result and a critique of the goals used to judge success. The authors conclude by discussing possible directions for addressing that gap.
icml-2025-revisiting-the-predictability-.tldr: Accurate, efficient prediction remains theoretically possible when forecasts shape social outcomes, but the resulting predictions can be undesirable.

paragraphs: Autoregressive emulators predict a system’s next state and repeatedly feed their predictions back into themselves. This can make simulation fast, but small errors accumulate during long rollouts and send trajectories outside the distribution the emulator handles well. Thermalizer addresses this instability in systems with turbulent or chaotic behavior.

The approach focuses on time-stationary systems that admit an invariant measure, a distribution preserved by the system’s dynamics. A diffusion model provides an implicit estimate of that distribution’s score function. During inference, the method applies denoising to the emulator’s evolving predictions. The authors call this ongoing correction thermalization and use it to stabilize the rollout.

The reported results extend the horizon of stable predictions by two orders of magnitude in complex turbulent and chaotic systems. This finding concerns how long the emulator remains stable, rather than asserting exact long-term trajectory recovery. The work demonstrates a role for diffusion models as inference-time stabilizers of another predictive model, using the system’s invariant distribution to counteract accumulated rollout errors.
icml-2025-thermalizer-stable-autoregress.tldr: For stationary systems with an invariant measure, diffusion-based denoising extends stable emulator rollouts by two orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: This paper studies training algorithms built around a linear minimization oracle over a norm-ball. Such an oracle chooses a direction by minimizing a linear objective within a region defined by a norm. The authors use this operation to construct a stochastic family of optimization methods that adapts to the geometry of a problem.

Although the oracle itself uses a constrained region, the resulting algorithms also apply to unconstrained optimization. Their update rule brings several existing methods into one framework. The paper additionally proposes a specific norm for deep architectures, with the useful consequence that hyperparameters can transfer across model sizes.

Experiments demonstrate significant training speedups on nanoGPT without relying on Adam. The proposed method requires storage for one set of model weights and one set of gradients, which can be kept in half precision. These results connect the geometric formulation to practical training concerns: computation time, memory use, and the effort involved in transferring optimizer settings between differently sized models.
icml-2025-training-deep-learning-models-.tldr: Norm-based linear minimization yields a unified, memory-efficient optimizer family with nanoGPT speedups and hyperparameter transfer across model sizes.

paragraphs: Wasserstein Policy Optimization, or WPO, is an actor-critic algorithm for reinforcement learning with continuous actions. Its derivation starts from Wasserstein gradient flow over the space of policies and approximates that flow after projection into a finite-dimensional parameter space, such as neural network weights. This produces a general closed-form update.

The resulting method combines properties associated with deterministic and classic policy gradients. It uses the gradient of the action-value function with respect to the action, allowing the update to exploit how value changes as an action changes. It can also train stochastic policies with arbitrary action distributions without requiring the reparameterization trick.

The authors evaluate WPO on the DeepMind Control Suite and a magnetic confinement fusion task, reporting results that compare favorably with state-of-the-art continuous control methods. The contribution is a policy update that connects distribution-level optimization with practical parameterized learning. Its combination of action-value gradients and support for general stochastic policies provides the central methodological motivation for the reported control experiments.
icml-2025-wasserstein-policy-optimizatio.tldr: WPO derives a continuous-control policy update that combines action-value gradients with support for arbitrary stochastic action distributions.
